historical_references.reference: Honorina, the first recorded British Christian martyr, was a young woman living in the Roman Empire during the early 4th century. She was the daughter of a Roman soldier and converted to Christianity after hearing the teachings of a local bishop. When her father discovered her new faith, he tried to dissuade her from her beliefs. Failing in this, he turned her over to the Roman authorities. She was imprisoned and tortured, but she refused to renounce her faith. Eventually, she was executed by being burned alive in a barrel. Her martyrdom is recorded in several early Christian texts, including the Acts of the Martyrs of Rome.

Honorina of Arles, also known as Honorina of Aix, was a Christian holy woman and martyr who lived in the late 5th century. She was the daughter of a wealthy nobleman in Gaul. According to legend, she was given in marriage to a pagan nobleman, but she refused to consummate the marriage or to participate in his pagan rituals. Her husband, in anger, reported her to the Roman authorities. She was imprisoned and tortured, but she refused to renounce her faith. Eventually, she was executed by being beheaded. Her cult became popular in the region, and she is venerated as a local saint.
